correctness.rationale: For n>=3 set m=n-2. At most one adjacent input can be used because deleting both ones gives the zero word. A near or far pair [i,j] can lose either one by starting the burst at i or j-1; the remaining positions are j-2 and i, coincident exactly at gap two. An adjacent pair has at least one external neighboring zero and hence consumes at least one of the m singleton outputs as well. Near starts two apart collide on a weight-two output, so their starts lie in independent sets on two parity paths. For m=4q+r the path bound is 2q plus 0,1,2,2 for r=0,1,2,3. Combining the singleton budget with this bound and the one-adjacent limit gives the claimed floor. In the stated construction singleton positions separate; zero-only bursts act before, between, or after the ones and give the eight distinct residue-pair types listed, with distinct absolute coordinates within each translated type. The boundary sizes and the three additional pairs per four positions check out. At n=2 there is one possible input. The supplied scripts were inspected, not run; the all-length proof is sufficient.

evidence: General adjacent burst constructions and redundancy bounds are not exact optimizations restricted to weight two. Constant-weight ordinary deletion colorings optimize a different graph. At n=4 the supports (0,2),(1,3) correct a two-burst but share an ordinary one-deletion output; at n=5 (0,1),(2,3) correct one deletion but share the zero two-burst output.
